description: The species I observed this week was a Mallard Duck (Anas platyrhynchos) while I was walking in Mill Creek Park the other day. I observed both a male and a female floating on the water. The males have a metallic green head, a white band on their neck, a brown chest, and a grey body. The females have a brown head and a brown body speckled with black markings. Both sexes have yellow beaks (females have brown on theirs) and orange feet. When they fly you can see a metallic blue stripe on their wing bordered by a white stripe on both sides. Mallards are dabbling ducks meaning they tip their bodies forward into the water to feed. Mallards like wetland areas, I spotted these particular Mallards in a lake that is surrounded by other waterways.  Another species I observed around the Mallard were Canada Geese (Branta canadensis). Canada Geese also live in wetland areas and I often spot these two species in close proximity of each other when I hike in this area. I believe they were both in the water feeding. The third species I identified this day around these birds was a Red Maple (Acer rubrum). This particular Red Maple had fallen in the water and some of the Mallards were perching on it. Red Maples grow in swampy areas and on streamsides, which is why I may have observed all these species together at a lake. The weather on the day I observed these species was sunny with no rain predicted for the day. The temperature at the time I made this observation was 38F, with a high for the day of 46F and a low of 27F. The wind was moving in a Northeastern direction at 3mph and the humidity was at 67%.

description:
Potential Mottled Duck on canal w/ 4 Mallard. Photos.

Compared to rubripes, overall paler aspect to the plumage, with warmer tones, paler crown, and warm buffy unstreaked throat and chin. Yellow bill with prominent black spot at the gape also a pro-fulvigula feature. Did not get a good look at the spread wing, but paler more turquoise tone of the speculum at some angles looked different to either rubripes or platyrhynchos. Did not see the thin white trailing edge evident in photos taken by others. No obvious signs of hybridization with platyrhynchos, such as white in tail or curly black uppertail coverts. Hard not to conclude this is fulvigula.

description: This is a pile of feathers on the ground in a deciduous forest on the shore of a lake where a large bird was apparently killed, or, at least plucked. The feathers appear to be from the torso of a mallard (or perhaps a Gadwall, although they are rare here). No large wing feathers, no carcass, no blood. There were no large overhead branches and the feathers were in a compact area, not scattered as if dropped from a height. They appeared to have been plucked, rather than chewed off. The quill on the long dark feather in the 4th picture appears pinched, which made me guess raptor for the predator. I would have guessed the predator was a fox, given that the carcass  was missing, but I wouldn’t expect a fox to pluck off body feathers before taking off with the carcass. Comments welcome.

White Rock lake, Sunset Bay
Photo 1:
Eyes Open
I was delighted to find a male green-winged teal at the lake.  I've only seen them a long way off before this one, it was much closer.  He had been napping but opened an eye when I showed up.  It was cold and cloudy, so the duck was all puffed up.  Showing just a bit of the green on the wing for which it is named.
Photo 2:
Eyes Shut
He decided I was no threat and closed his eye.  Looked a bit weird because his eyelid is white.  I've seen this in pintail ducks too.  At first I would think there was something wrong with their eye.  Finally realized it was just white eyelids.

description: I observed an Anas platyrhynchos, commonly named as the Mallard, that was walking around a lake located inside a residential community. This organism is labeled within the Genus Anas, consisting of many ducks that spend a majority of their time swimming in aquatic habitats, sometimes on land. Its head is an emerald green color along with a white ring separating the neck and body, which has various colorations such as white, gray, brown, light brown, blue, and back with sprouting feathers towards its tail. Additionally, its legs were a bright orange color with webbed feet that allow it to swim easily and a yellow beak. This species can be found in a large array of locations including Europe, Asia, and most of North America. This is due to the species being an ancestor to so many other breeds of lucks found in today's modern society. Its taxonomic groups include being in the Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Aves, Order Anseriformes, Family Anatidae, Genus Anas, and Species platyrhynchos. The website https://invasions.si.edu/nemesis/chesreport/species_summary/Anas%20platyrhynchos#:~:text=Anas%20platyrhynchos(Mallard%20Duck)%20is,North%20America%20is%20somewhat%20obscure. provides specific information on its uniqueness and how it can be compared to other similar species.

description:
in 2021 a pair of odd ducks showed up at this park, although they may have been around earlier than that based on earlier observations that you can find here.  eventually they were identified by experts as the male being a mexican and the female being a mexican x mottled hybrid, and you can look up pictures of them all on ebird. no sightings have been confirmed recently but the chipped bill on the female is in the same place and odds are it proves they are the same individuals. letha sagle and mark kulstad's notes on them are really detailed and it's what I used to distinguish all the mottled/mallards/mallard/mottled hybrids that could easily be around. pair of similar small mottled ducks that I saw had the typical wing pattern that eliminated them as they flew. 

female has darker cap like male. mostly orange bill and lacks black spotting. in good sunlight female wing panel is more teal/turquoise colored than mottled, and also has white rim. female has darker face than the male, also has streaking pattern on top and then becomes more buffy at the bottom. has very little black on gape. apparently mottled x mexican is not on inaturalist so I will probably end up keeping it at genus level.

Deuterostome

Habitat where it lives- lives on land but near water sites, the specimens were found at park right next to the beach in St. Petersburg. They are common in wetlands and will commonly be found in lakes, rivers, ponds, or even beaches. 
Range of where it can be found- this species can be found throughout North America and Eurasia, in parks, ponds, and estuaries. 
Defining characteristics of of higher taxon- they possess a beak, feathers, lay eggs and can fly, therefore, belonging in the phylum chordata and Aves class .

description:
On January 1st, @blazeclaw posted https://forum.inaturalist.org/t/operation-dethrone-mallard-2022/28761 in the forum. Operation Dethrone Mallard was viewed 2,500 times and trending for a while. Ever since, my Mallard postings were deliberate and came with a mental or actual note about their importance. Like this one.

I found these two Mallards in the "Water Garden" of a dot com high rises campus. Water and Garden in Santa Monica sounded promising, sounded like it was designed with wildlife in mind. After wandering around for a while, I finally found these two Mallards next to a fountain, and at first thought they must be rubber ducks, because the area was so sterile and unsuitable. But it looked like they had made a home there, and were even very tolerant of a little boy who petted them. Several people stopped by and took pictures. When I was on my way out, the Mallards were paddling in the fountain.

These ducks who are so tolerant of us could hopefully be an introduction to wildlife for many people. And I was just so very glad to see them.

(Eventually, I also saw two House Finches, two Dark-eyed Juncos, heard Lesser Goldfinches, and saw and heard the pendulum flight of two male Allen's Hummingbirds in between the planted bottle brushes.)
